Café culture is part of daily life in many cities. In Paris, people linger over an espresso and a croissant, and in Vienna a waiter might bring a glass of water on a silver tray. Naïve travelers sometimes ask for the bill too early. “Take your time,” the waiter says, and no one is in a hurry.

Math symbols appear in books too: π ≈ 3.14159, the square root of two is √2, and 5 × 4 ÷ 2 = 10. If x ≤ 7 and y ≥ 3, then x + y is at least 3. A triangle’s angles add up to 180°, and ½ plus ¼ equals ¾.

Emoji are tiny pictures that people use in messages. Here are some: 🙂 😀 😂 🎉 🚀 🌈 🐱 🐶 🍕 🍎 ☀️ ⭐ ❤️ 👍 🌍 📚 🎵. A sentence can end with a smile 🙂 or with a rocket 🚀. Birthday messages are full of balloons 🎈 and cake 🎂, and a rainy day gets an umbrella ☔.

Mixed text happens in real chat: “I’m heading to the café with Zoë — meet me there 🙂.” She replied, “Sure! 日本のお菓子も持っていくね 🍡.” Names such as José, Łukasz, Dvořák, and Nguyễn are written the same way everywhere, and the tokenizer must keep every single byte.

Some special characters are easy to lose: a non-breaking space between words, an en dash for ranges like 10–20, an em dash — like this — for a pause, and the ellipsis… at the end of a thought. Curly quotes ‘single’ and “double” are different from the straight ones that you type with a plain keyboard.

Tabs	separate	columns,	and	line endings can be different on different systems. Trailing spaces matter too.   Text with extra   spaces must still round-trip exactly.
